idiom_name: enum with associated values + exhaustive switch (indirect for recursion)
implementation_notes: Swift enums are sum types with value semantics: `enum Payment { case card(number: String); case transfer(iban: String) }` fixes the case set, every case carries its own associated values, and the compiler *requires* a `switch` over the enum to be exhaustive - a missing case is a compile error, so no `default` is needed. `let` bindings and value semantics supply the immutability half (cases are copied, not shared), `indirect` marks recursive cases (the `Tree`/expression-tree shape), and `@unknown default` exists only for nonfrozen enums, where it warns when it shadows a known case. The classic class-cluster structure (private init plus subclasses, or a tag plus payload struct) remains the fallback when cases must be reference types or are exported to Objective-C, whose enums cannot carry associated values.
pitfalls: Nonfrozen enums (libraries in library-evolution mode, C/Objective-C enums) require a `default`/`@unknown default` arm, and it will absorb future cases - only `@unknown default` warns when it shadows a known case.
Recursive cases must be marked `indirect` (on the case or the whole enum) or the type fails to compile; the indirection boxes the associated value, so deep structures allocate on the heap.
Associated values are copied, but reference-type payloads (classes, closures) are shared and stay mutable - value semantics stop at the top level.
Switching over an optional enum needs an explicit `nil` case, because `Optional` is itself an enum.
